note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — HAIRY BLADE BASE
tiles.details: Spread an attached mature leaf at the sheath mouth. A dense triangular or cup-shaped white silky hair patch supports switchgrass; it is NOT the ligule itself and is NOT a true auricle. Existing source-identified collar photo shows real hairs with a 5-mm reference, but the tiny membrane edge is still not independently pixel-certified. Check more than one leaf.
tiles.short: Expose the triangular WHITE HAIR PATCH on the UPPER leaf blade base.
tiles.status: VISIBLE COLLAR HAIRS — TRUE MEMBRANE EDGE HOLD

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE LIGULE AND ROOTED BASE
tiles.details: Lift the hair tuft to expose the short true membranous ligule beneath; photograph its actual edge at 10–20× with a 0.5–1-mm reference. Bob Harms's credited educational-use opened collar plate is genuine anatomy, but exact membrane-tip arrow placement remains unverified. The physically archived Austrian rhizome photo shows an attached underground stem, not a Texas voucher; upland plants may have short rhizomes.
tiles.short: Short ciliate membranous ligule; perennial with scaly rhizomes.
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE COLLAR/RHIZOME IMAGES — LOCAL SAME-PLANT GAP

tiles.heading: 03 · FOLLOW THE ENTIRE PANICLE
tiles.details: Trace one mature culm from upper leaf to its entire many-branched panicle; the existing whole-panicle and flowering branch photographs demonstrate the architecture. Individual spikelets occur singly on slender pedicels, not as the conspicuous fertile sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs of Johnsongrass. Purple feathery structures visible in the flowering photo are STIGMAS, not awns; measure 5–10 ripe spikelets with a 1-mm scale.
tiles.short: Broad open pyramidal panicle ~15–55 cm; single AWNLESS ~3–5 mm spikelets.
tiles.status: SOURCE PHOTOS SHOW ARCHITECTURE — RIPE LOCAL SCALE GAP

tiles.heading: 04 · OPEN ONE MATURE SPIKELET
tiles.details: At 10–20× remove one mature ~3–5 mm spikelet and identify both enclosing glumes, the lower sterile/staminate floret's lemma and the firm upper fertile floret's lemma plus palea. The source-labelled sl53 real photographed dissection labels Glu, Lem and Pal; the physically archived author-labelled dissection is not a locally vouchered measured Hays specimen. The enclosed fertile-floret image is separately archived. No conspicuous lemma awn; never label the stalk or stigma as an awn.
tiles.short: Separate two glumes, lower sterile/staminate floret and upper fertile lemma/palea.
tiles.status: ACTUAL SOURCE DISSECTION — SAME-TEXAS-SPECIMEN PHOTO GAP

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans) often has a tall notched 'rifle-sight' membrane, narrower tawny panicle and bent awned spikelets. Introduced Johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense) also has a broad panicle and rhizomes, but its reproductive spikelet pairs differ. Hall's panicgrass is usually smaller and stiffer with basal leaves; witchgrass is a hairy annual; introduced kleingrass has a knotty tuft and smaller spikelets. Collar hair or panicle width alone is insufficient.
tiles.short: Indiangrass has a tall notched ligule and bent awns; Johnsongrass has paired spikelets.
tiles.status: PRACTICAL LOOK-ALIKE KEY — MATCHED LOCAL PHOTOS NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY PHOTO AND QA GATE
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one determined Central Texas rooted plant with rhizome-to-culm-to-panicle continuity (cm scale); true short membrane edge under the hair patch with 0.5–1-mm scale; 5–10 mature 3–5 mm spikelets, opened glumes and lower/upper lemmas with paleas at 10–20×; matched Indiangrass/Johnsongrass collars and ripe heads. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify all ten existing image records and actual physical/external paths, CC/PD/Bob Harms educational-only attribution, existing original and newly verified gross arrows and mobile responsive page. Keep new arrows source-pixel-reviewed, but mobile/public-page QA remains open. Do not assert FINISHED.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS; source photos do not equal 100% verified anatomy.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: SWITCHGRASS — LOOK FIRST AT THE UPPER SURFACE OF A LEAF WHERE IT MEETS THE SHEATH. A conspicuous triangular, often white 'HAIRY ARMPIT' occurs at the blade base; beneath/between the hairs is a SHORT ciliate MEMBRANOUS LIGULE, not Indiangrass's tall pointed 'rifle-sight' membrane. Turn to the seedhead: an expansive AIRY, broad triangular/pyramidal BRANCHED PANICLE with individual small, AWNLESS, typically 3–5 mm spikelets on stalks. Finally examine a many-stemmed warm-season perennial with scaly rhizomes (or compact rhizomatous crown in upland types). Compare true Indiangrass's narrower golden feathery panicle and bent awned spikelets, Johnsongrass's developed spikelet pairs and creeping rhizomes, and the smaller/tufted Panicum hallii. Collar hairs alone do NOT prove switchgrass: look for the combined hairy triangular blade base, shorter ciliolate membrane, panicle structure and awnless spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FIRST examine the archived switchgrass stand, then the physically archived Stefan.lefnaer source-identified rhizome WITH the basal shoots and fine roots attached. This is real perennial growth structure, but the specimen was photographed outside Texas and not linked to a full locally vouchered flowering culm.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Spread an attached mature leaf at the sheath mouth. A dense triangular or cup-shaped white silky hair patch supports switchgrass; it is NOT the ligule itself and is NOT a true auricle. Existing source-identified collar photo shows real hairs with a 5-mm reference, but the tiny membrane edge is still not independently pixel-certified. Check more than one leaf.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Trace one mature culm from upper leaf to its entire many-branched panicle; the existing whole-panicle and flowering branch photographs demonstrate the architecture. Individual spikelets occur singly on slender pedicels, not as the conspicuous fertile sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs of Johnsongrass. Purple feathery structures visible in the flowering photo are STIGMAS, not awns; measure 5–10 ripe spikelets with a 1-mm scale.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: FIRST expose the triangular HAIR PATCH at the upper leaf blade base and the much shorter ciliate membrane (no stiff rifle-sight projection). NEXT trace the broad AIRY panicle and separate single unawned small spikelets. Indiangrass has a taller notched membranous collar, narrower tawny panicle and BENT AWNS; Johnsongrass has a large open panicle too but fertile sessile/pedicelled pairs and robust rhizomes, lacking the distinctive triangular hair patch. Hall's panicgrass is generally smaller and bluer with basal leaves and shorter stiffly branching panicle; witchgrass is a hairy annual with an extremely diffuse irregular panicle; kleingrass is an introduced tufted perennial with a knotty crown. No cultivar IDs from leaf color.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.caption: DIFFERENT SPECIES — Indiangrass. This licensed Matt Lavin collar photo shows a very different leaf junction: a projecting rifle-sight membrane/collar region and sheath corners. panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE (different species) · Florida paspalum coarse clump
panels.caption: DIFFERENT SPECIES — Florida paspalum. A similarly robust grass clump can resemble switchgrass if neither is blooming. Florida paspalum's true flowering racemes and larger paired flattened one-sided spikelets are decisive; its brown membranous ligule requires a separate actual collar photo. This broad clump picture does NOT demonstrate that membrane.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE · JOHNSONGRASS hairy collar — DIFFERENT SPECIES
panels.caption: DIFFERENT SPECIES — introduced Johnsongrass, photographed by Matt Lavin. The collar has a hairy ligule region, so a tuft of hairs BY ITSELF does not separate this grass from switchgrass. Check the full panicle and mature spikelets: Johnsongrass has paired sessile/pedicelled spikelets; switchgrass has individual awnless spikelets on delicate pedicels. This photograph does not reveal that panicle difference.

Compare true Indiangrass's narrower golden feathery panicle and bent awned spikelets, Johnsongrass's developed spikelet pairs and creeping rhizomes, and the smaller/tufted Panicum hallii. memory_rule: MEMBRANE != WHITE HAIRS: true Panicum virgatum ligule consists of a short ciliate membrane with longer white silky hairs around/behind it; membrane can weather off on older leaves. Open the leaf sheath gently to locate it, and compare Harms dissected plate with the actual sl37 hair photograph.
safety_note: TEN physically archived exact-species JPEGs now verified in GitHub, including basal rhizome, entire attached upper panicle, original labeled wide spikelet dissection and enclosed fertile-floret macro; plus three species-labelled look-alike gallery panels stored in other species folders. One existing Bob Harms locally copied image carries scoped copyrighted scientific/educational use, NOT CC; no new Harms image copying/annotations authorized by the reviewed memo. Original thin membrane tip and Hays same-root-to-flower specimen missing. Neither the latest site snapshot SHA nor mobile responsive arrow QA is proven by this commit.
field_rule: SWITCHGRASS = HAIRY TRIANGLE at blade base + AIRY PANICLE + AWNLESS single spikelets.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
